newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end higher on weather, demand ideas.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end higher on weather, demand ideas.

text.p: Forecasts for a cool and wet week in the U.S. Midwest and ideas demand remained strong for tight supplies pushed CBOT soybean futures to a higher close, pit sources said.

Meteorologists said colder weather would follow a warm weekend. That scenario suggested soybean plantings would slow. Trade sources expected Monday's USDA weekly crop progress report to show 20 to 25 percent of the crop planted.
Ideas demand continued to run strong were supported by the National Oilseed Processors Association weekly crush figures and a spike in U.S. Gulf CIF values.
NOPA put the crush at 24.6 million bushels, at the high end of trade expectations.

"We did have a pretty good sized crush," said Jason Roose, analyst with U.S. Commodities in Iowa. "People are saying it's below a year ago, but you have to remember we did not have a 125 million carryover last year."
Also, U.S. Gulf May CIF values rose by two to three cents per bushel Friday morning. Exporters cited lack of farmer selling and strong processor demand in domestic U.S. markets.
Soybeans ended 6-3/4 to one cent per bushel higher with July up five at $8.89.
Trade sources said the CIF action primarily affected the May/July spread. The May gained 1-3/4 cents on the July and the spread closed at 5-1/4 cents, premium May.

The May was further supported by a cut in registered soybean stocks. Deliverable stocks fell by 500,000 bushels in Toledo. The move suggested demand in the country was strong enough to pull soybeans away from the delivery market, pit sources said.

Trade was said to be thin ahead of Monday's USDA supply and demand report. Trade sources predicted USDA would trim five million to 10 million bushels off of an already tight ending stocks projection of 125 million bushels.

On the day, ADM bought 3.5 million bushels July and Refco Inc bought 1.5 million July, traders said. FIMAT Futures sold three million bushels November and ABN-AMRO Chicago Corp sold two million November.
Spread trade was again active, most notably in the July/November spread. Lee B. Stern spread one million bushels July/November at $1.75 to $1.74-1/2, premium July.
In options, Rand Financial bought 600 August $8.25 puts at 27-1/2 cents and Louis Dreyfus bought 400 July $8.75 puts at 26-1/2 to 27 cents.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 60,000 contracts, compared with Thursday's actual volume of 56,298 contracts.
